snippet.title: How Companies From Apple To Pfizer Use Ireland To Dodge Taxes
snippet.description:
A range of U.S. businesses store intellectual property in Ireland due to a favorable business environment built on low corporate taxes. Examples are common in the technology and pharmaceutical industries. In recent years, a global push to establish minimum corporate tax rates led Ireland to revise its codes. But loopholes remain, urging officials in the U.S. to re-examine this long-standing relationship.

snippet.title: The Delaware Loophole: America’s Hidden Tax Haven Exposed
snippet.description:
Why are more than a million companies—from Wall Street giants to Silicon Valley startups—incorporated in a single tiny state?

This deep-dive unpacks how Delaware quietly became America’s corporate tax haven, earning the nickname “The Cayman Islands of Wall Street.” From secret shell companies and Fortune 500 tax tricks, to Elon Musk pulling Tesla out of Delaware after a $56 billion court ruling, this story reveals the hidden system shaping American business.

We’ll cover:
 • Why two-thirds of the Fortune 500 are incorporated in Delaware
 • How the “Delaware loophole” lets companies dodge billions in taxes
 • The rise of shell companies, secrecy, and global money flows
 • Why Musk, Tesla, and others are leaving Delaware behind
 • The future of America’s shadow banking system

This isn’t just about corporate law—it’s about who writes the rules of capitalism, and who pays the price.

snippet.title: What EVE Online's Tax Havens Teach Us About New York's Future
snippet.description:
Sign up for my newsletter https://compoundeddaily.com 👈

-----

This is the largest trade hub in EVE online, A massively multiplayer spaceship game with by far the most realistic financial system in the virtual world. And this is downtown Manhattan, the largest trade hub, in well, the real world. 

These two regions of concentrated commerce have more than you might expect in common and what has happened before in this virtual world, might be a very good indication of what end’s up happening here in the real world. 

But we are getting ahead of ourselves. 

In our last video in this series we explored how eve online’s massive in game wars were financed, and at a cost of hundreds of thousands or even millions of dollars… why they were financed…

Now a few people reached out to me after that video and said I missed a very interesting detail, the battle over in game tax havens. 

You see when a financial system is as realistic as the one in EVE Online, it comes with some unfortunate realities as well, most notably, needing to work hard to make in game money, currency inflation and of course paying taxes…


So it’s time to learn how money works and take a look at the different taxes players in eve online are expected to pay, how they avoid paying them, and what this can teach us about the fate of New York.

snippet.title: There’s nothing in a tax haven
snippet.description:
I keep hearing people say that we need to get the money back from tax havens. That, though, is not necessary. There is no money in tax havens. All they do is record the ownership of money and other funds that are always actually deposited elsewhere, like the City of London. Instead, what we want back from them is the tax not paid on income recorded there as a consequence of this.

snippet.title: How and Why Corporations Use Tax Havens
snippet.description:
Corporate tax avoidance: What it is, how it happens and why it concerns governments. 

Ana Maria Santacreu, an economist at the St. Louis Fed, describes profit shifting: Multinational firms can avoid corporate taxes by shifting their intellectual property rights—and the ensuing profits—to their subsidiaries in lower-tax jurisdictions. Estimates put the lost tax revenue in the U.S. at over $100 billion annually. The views expressed in this video do not necessarily reflect those of the St. Louis Fed or the Federal Reserve System.

The main objective was to reduce profit shifting and tax avoidance by setting a minimum tax of 15% on corporate profits regardless of where these profits had been originated. And the OECD estimated that as a result of this agreement, there would be an additional US$150 billion in global tax revenues worldwide and annually. 

So what is profit shifting? And why are governments concerned about this activity? Profit shifting is a strategic approach that is used by multinational corporations in high tax jurisdictions to move their location of their profits to low tax jurisdictions and in that way they can minimize their tax liability. There are estimates that indicate that 37% of multinational profits in 2019 were moved to tax havens worldwide. For instance, recent estimates suggest that profit shifting could have caused the U.S. prior to 2017 over US$100 billion in corporate tax revenues annually. 

So how does this work in practice? Take for example the case of a U.S. pharma multinational that develops a groundbreaking medicine. The way they would do that is by opening a subsidiary in Ireland, sending the ownership of the patent to the Irish subsidiary. This Irish subsidiary would have all the rights to use this technology to produce the drug, and they could license this technology to other countries. 

The subsidiary in Ireland would be getting royalty payments instead of the U.S. company getting royalty payments. And these royalty payments in Ireland would be taxed at a lower tax rate. In that way, what the company is doing is moving profits from the U.S., taxed at a higher tax rate, into Ireland, which would be taxed at a lower tax rate. 

The reason why firms engage in profit shifting practices in this way is because it's easier to move intellectual property than to move tangible assets. Intellectual property is an intangible and that's easier to move around countries than, say, selling factories or moving machinery or equipment. Now, despite the simplicity, these activities can get quite complex very quickly because they tend to involve many countries, making it challenging for governments to address effectively. 

And these practices are not limited to the pharmaceutical industry. They tend to happen in sectors that have a global presence and that have a lot of intangible assets. So they tend to happen in sectors like pharmaceutical and technology, but also in sectors like media, entertainment, retail, banking, and energy.

And these questions deserve further investigation.

▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀

The Netherlands, a fine country of flowers, windmills, and loose regulations around the finer things in life. This country is in many ways like a lot of very developed European economies we have explored earlier on the channel, very high living standards, good social mobility a strong economy and healthy inequality but the Netherlands hides a bit of a secret behind its lovely flowerful smile, it is one of the largest tax havens in the world. 

But how does this make any sense? The Netherlands has a high-income tax rate of over 50% for top earners and a corporate tax rate of 25%. And there are not even particularly strict laws around things like banking privacy (like there are in countries like Switzerland) ... so if all of this is making the Netherlands sound like a pretty terrible tax haven all in all, why is it so popular?

snippet.description:
"Why do tiny islands with almost no population control trillions of dollars in global wealth?.
In this Financial Mindset deep-dive, we uncover the hidden world of tax havens and offshore finance. From the Cayman Islands and Bermuda to Switzerland, Luxembourg, and the British Virgin Islands, certain countries built entire economies around attracting billionaire wealth, multinational corporations, hedge funds, and offshore profits.
This video explains:
\What tax havens actually are
\Why billionaires and corporations move money offshore
\How countries like Cayman and Bermuda became global financial centers
\The role of shell companies, trusts, and offshore banking
\How multinational corporations legally reduce taxes
\The truth behind the Panama Papers and Pandora Papers
\Why governments struggle to stop offshore wealth protection
\How global tax competition reshaped the modern economy
\We also break down how corporations shift profits using intellectual property, subsidiaries, and legal loopholes across multiple countries
\This isn’t just about hidden bank accounts.
\It’s about power, global finance, and a system where money moves faster than governments can regulate it
\As nations attempt to impose global minimum taxes and tighten regulations, offshore finance continues evolving
\Because in the modern world, some of the most powerful financial centers aren’t giant countries
\They’re tiny islands protecting global wealth.
Watch till the end to understand how tax havens became one of the most influential systems in the global economy.

snippet.title: The Bizarre Economics of Tax Havens and Pirate Banking: James S. Henry at TEDxRadboudU 2013
snippet.description:
James S. Henry introduces a hot topic: offshore banking. The G8 and G20 are planning meetings to discuss it. Even the Netherlands is a tax haven for certain types of companies. The huge amount of numbers and graphs tells us that we are confronted with nothing less than a global tax haven industry. For example, Apple makes 100 billion dollars a year of tax free profits because of the games private bankers know how to play.

In medieval times people couldn't hide their wealth when tax collectors came to inventory it. Nowadays they can. It is said that 64 percent of the global profits are parked offshore, for an important part by multinationals from the first world.

The third world is the victim of this practise. An example from the banana industry: exporting a banana from the Cayman Islands costs 13 pence. When it arrives in the UK to be consumed, the costs have grown to 60 pence. All of this money goes to other parties than the Cayman Islands.

Because of the tax havens, countries from the Third World are not able to receive the tax incomes they are entitled to. Henry even concludes that the debt problem of the third world is not a debt problem, but a tax problem. Both amount to almost the same.
